PFS and OS tested together

Source: vignettes/two-endpoints.Rmd
two-endpoints.Rmd
library(DesignComplexSurvival)

Progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) come from the same multistate model, so that their log-rank statistics are correlated. The package computes the joint distribution of the two statistics over calendar time and tests the two hypotheses with a group sequential fixed-sequence or Bonferroni procedure, the latter with recycling of the level after a rejection.

Scenario and analyses

Both groups follow the model of Fleischer et al. (2009): the times to progression and to death are exponential and the hazard of death does not change at progression, so that PFS and OS are exponential. The medians of PFS and OS are 4 and 12 months in the control group and 6 and 16 months in the treatment group, and 450 patients are enrolled at 25 per month.

PFS is tested at 300 PFS events, where OS is also tested, and OS is tested again at 220 OS events. Each look has its own trigger, and test lists the endpoints tested at each look:

fl <- ms_scenario(ms_fleischer(median_pfs = 4, median_os = 12),
                  ms_fleischer(median_pfs = 6, median_os = 16),
                  accrual = ms_accrual(rate = 25))
lk2 <- ms_looks(c("pfs", "os"), fraction = c(1, 1),
                test = list(c("pfs", "os"), "os"))
ev2 <- c(pfs = 300, os = 220)

Fixed sequence

With the fixed-sequence procedure, both hypotheses are tested at level 0.025 and OS is tested only after PFS has been rejected: at the analysis at which PFS is rejected and at the later analyses (procedure (b) of Glimm et al. 2010, hierarchical = "overall"). Each endpoint has its own efficacy bounds of O’Brien-Fleming type.

fs <- ms_power(fl, n = 450, looks = lk2,
               test = ms_test(endpoints = c("pfs", "os"), mtp = "fixed_sequence"),
               events = ev2)
fs
#> Group sequential log-rank design with two endpoints
#>   Endpoints: PFS, then OS (fixed sequence, overall); looks driven by PFS events and OS events
#>   Sample size: 450; accrual duration: 18; final analysis at: 23.05
#>   Power: PFS 0.9387, OS 0.5452; both 0.5452; at least one 0.9387
#>   FWER under global null: 0.025 (non-binding), 0.025 (binding)
#>  endpoint look  time events info_frac z_upper  p_upper hr_upper z_lower
#>       PFS    1 18.62    300    1.0000   1.960 0.025000   0.7975   1.960
#>        OS    1 18.62    163    0.7407   2.357 0.009207   0.6912    -Inf
#>        OS    2 23.05    220    1.0000   2.009 0.022243   0.7626   2.009
#>  hr_lower prob_upper prob_lower cum_power
#>    0.7975     0.9387          0    0.9387
#>        NA     0.2966          0    0.2966
#>    0.7626     0.2486          0    0.5452

The power is 0.939 for PFS and 0.545 for OS, and both hypotheses are rejected with probability 0.545. The final OS analysis takes place at month 23.1.

With hierarchical = "stagewise", OS is tested only at the analysis at which PFS is rejected, where the trial stops (procedure (a) of Glimm et al. 2010; Tamhane et al. 2010). Here PFS is tested at the first analysis only, so OS can be rejected only there:

fs_a <- ms_power(fl, n = 450, looks = lk2,
                 test = ms_test(endpoints = c("pfs", "os"), mtp = "fixed_sequence",
                                hierarchical = "stagewise"),
                 events = ev2)
rbind(overall = fs$power, stagewise = fs_a$power)
#>                 pfs        os      both       any
#> overall   0.9387378 0.5451639 0.5451639 0.9387378
#> stagewise 0.9387378 0.2965913 0.2965913 0.9387378

Bonferroni and recycling of the level

The Bonferroni procedure with the weights 0.8 and 0.2 tests PFS at level 0.02 and OS at level 0.005, whatever happens to the other hypothesis. With transition in ms_test() the level of a rejected hypothesis is passed on to the other in the graphical procedure of Maurer and Bretz (2013). With transition = c(1, 1), OS is tested at level 0.025 once PFS has been rejected, and PFS at level 0.025 once OS has been rejected.

bf <- ms_power(fl, n = 450, looks = lk2,
               test = ms_test(endpoints = c("pfs", "os"), mtp = "bonferroni",
                              weights = c(0.8, 0.2)),
               events = ev2)
rc <- ms_power(fl, n = 450, looks = lk2,
               test = ms_test(endpoints = c("pfs", "os"), mtp = "bonferroni",
                              weights = c(0.8, 0.2), transition = c(1, 1)),
               events = ev2)
rbind(fixed_sequence = fs$power, bonferroni = bf$power, recycling = rc$power)
#>                      pfs        os      both       any
#> fixed_sequence 0.9387378 0.5451639 0.5451639 0.9387378
#> bonferroni     0.9265375 0.3237669 0.3173922 0.9329122
#> recycling      0.9266956 0.5479409 0.5417243 0.9329122
rc$looks[, c("endpoint", "look", "time", "z_upper", "z_upper_recycled",
             "p_upper", "p_upper_recycled")]
#>   endpoint look     time  z_upper z_upper_recycled     p_upper p_upper_recycled
#> 1      pfs    1 18.62269 2.053749         1.959964 0.020000000      0.025000000
#> 2       os    1 18.62269 3.059549         2.357185 0.001108353      0.009207032
#> 3       os    2 23.05363 2.600794         2.009474 0.004650414      0.022243431

The power for OS is 0.324 without and 0.548 with recycling. The columns z_upper_recycled and p_upper_recycled give the bounds at the level after the other hypothesis has been rejected. The procedure controls the familywise error rate when the nominal levels of the spending functions do not decrease with the level (Maurer and Bretz 2013, Section 3.1), and ms_power() checks at every look that the bounds after recycling do not exceed the bounds at the initial level.

Familywise error rate

The familywise error rate is computed under the global null hypothesis, where the correlation between the PFS and OS statistics is that of Danzer et al. (2025, Theorem 1). A partial null hypothesis, in which OS is the same in both groups but PFS is not, cannot be derived from the design scenario and is given through null_scenarios:

os_null <- ms_scenario(ms_fleischer(median_pfs = 4, median_os = 12),
                       ms_fleischer(median_pfs = 6, median_os = 12),
                       accrual = ms_accrual(rate = 25))
fw <- ms_power(fl, n = 450, looks = lk2,
               test = ms_test(endpoints = c("pfs", "os"), mtp = "fixed_sequence"),
               events = ev2, null_scenarios = list(os = os_null))
fw$fwer
#>              scenario null_endpoints nonbinding    binding
#> 1              global        PFS, OS 0.02500000 0.02500000
#> 2 null_scenarios[[1]]             OS 0.02405394 0.02405394

An interim analysis of PFS

The following design adds an interim analysis of PFS at 60 percent of the PFS events, as in the example of ms_looks():

lk3 <- ms_looks(c("pfs", "pfs", "os"), fraction = c(0.6, 1, 1),
                test = list("pfs", c("pfs", "os"), "os"))
fs3 <- ms_power(fl, n = 450, looks = lk3,
                test = ms_test(endpoints = c("pfs", "os"), mtp = "fixed_sequence"),
                events = ev2)
fs3$looks[, c("endpoint", "look", "trigger", "time", "events", "z_upper",
              "prob_upper")]
#>   endpoint look trigger     time   events  z_upper prob_upper
#> 1      pfs    1     pfs 13.17448 180.0000 2.668630  0.5180390
#> 2      pfs    2     pfs 18.62269 300.0000 1.980965  0.4190402
#> 3       os    2     pfs 18.62269 162.9636 2.357185  0.2964566
#> 4       os    3      os 23.05363 220.0000 2.009474  0.2482003
rbind(two_analyses = fs$power, three_analyses = fs3$power)
#>                      pfs        os      both       any
#> two_analyses   0.9387378 0.5451639 0.5451639 0.9387378
#> three_analyses 0.9370793 0.5446569 0.5446569 0.9370793

The interim analysis of PFS takes place at month 13.2. Futility bounds, when given, are placed on the first endpoint of the test.

Correlation between the statistics

lr_cov() gives the joint distribution of the statistics. At month 24 the correlation between the PFS and OS statistics is

cv <- lr_cov(fl, n = 450, calendar_time = 24, endpoint = c("pfs", "os"),
             variance = "studentized")
cv0 <- lr_cov(ms_null(fl), n = 450, calendar_time = 24, endpoint = c("pfs", "os"))
c(design = stats::cov2cor(cv$sigma)[1, 2], global_null = stats::cov2cor(cv0$sigma)[1, 2])
#>      design global_null 
#>   0.4518932   0.4204810

ms_size() finds the sample size, number of events, accrual duration or follow-up for a target power of the first endpoint, of each endpoint, of both or of at least one (argument target).

References

Danzer MF, Rufibach K, Beyersmann J, Schmidt R (2025). Exhausting the type I error level in event-driven group-sequential designs with a closed testing procedure for progression-free and overall survival. arXiv:2512.08658.

Fleischer F, Gaschler-Markefski B, Bluhmki E (2009). A statistical model for the dependence between progression-free survival and overall survival. Statistics in Medicine 28:2669-2686.

Glimm E, Maurer W, Bretz F (2010). Hierarchical testing of multiple endpoints in group-sequential trials. Statistics in Medicine 29:219-228.

Maurer W, Bretz F (2013). Multiple testing in group sequential trials using graphical approaches. Statistics in Biopharmaceutical Research 5:311-320.

Tamhane AC, Mehta CR, Liu L (2010). Testing a primary and a secondary endpoint in a group sequential design. Biometrics 66:1174-1184.
